---
applyTo: "**/src/main/mule/**/*.xml,**/src/main/resources/log4j2.xml"

# Mule XML changes

Follow the project's existing structure and conventions first. Links below are Mule 4.9 examples; use documentation for the project's runtime.

## Correctness and safety

- Inspect neighboring configuration and declared connector versions first. Confirm XML elements, namespaces, configuration references, and error types against the applicable version's documentation; do not invent an element because its name seems plausible.
- Preserve the API contract and established flow boundaries. Reuse existing global configurations and externalized properties. Do not generate credentials or realistic private endpoints.
- Give every processor a descriptive `doc:name`; readers and MUnit mocks identify processors by it. Keep APIkit-generated flows thin, each calling an implementation flow through `flow-ref`, so the scaffolding can be regenerated when the API specification changes.
- Prefer the approved Validation module for new input checks when it fits the contract. Replacing Choice plus `raise-error` can change the error type; preserve the existing type and response contract through error mapping, and do not add a dependency just to rewrite a working check. Set a conditional value with one DataWeave `if`/`else` when equivalent; keep Choice for routing. See [Validation errors](https://docs.mulesoft.com/validation-connector/2.0/validation-documentation), [error mapping](https://docs.mulesoft.com/mule-runtime/4.9/mule-error-concept) and [app design for performance](https://docs.mulesoft.com/mule-runtime/4.9/tuning-app-design).
- Retry only when the operation and failure mode justify it; account for duplicate side effects and the established idempotency contract. Do not wrap every connector call in retries. HTTP `GET`, `PUT` and `DELETE` have idempotent method semantics; `POST` and `PATCH` are not guaranteed idempotent, so verify the API's retry contract, including any idempotency keys or preconditions. Updates across several systems are not one transaction: when a later step fails, define compensating actions for the steps that succeeded. Until Successful re-runs everything inside it up to `maxRetries` times and then raises `MULE:RETRY_EXHAUSTED`; keep only idempotent operations inside it and handle that error. See [Until Successful](https://docs.mulesoft.com/mule-runtime/4.9/until-successful-scope). Do not add parallelism or change ordering without an explicit requirement and tests.
- Preserve approved secret injection and TLS validation. Do not commit decryption keys, introduce trust-all settings, or set `disableCertificateValidation`/insecure options anywhere, including log appenders, to make something work. Encrypted values use the `![…]` form in a file loaded by `secure-properties:config`. Use `${secure::key}` for every value loaded by that provider, including unencrypted values; plain `${key}` is not an equivalent lookup. Supply the decryption key through the project's runtime secret mechanism, never in the repository; do not assume CloudHub's hidden-property behavior applies to hybrid deployments. See [secure properties](https://docs.mulesoft.com/mule-runtime/4.9/secure-configuration-properties), [safely hidden properties](https://docs.mulesoft.com/cloudhub-1/secure-application-properties) and [TLS](https://docs.mulesoft.com/mule-runtime/4.9/tls-configuration).
- Log approved operational metadata, such as a non-sensitive correlation ID and outcome. When some payload content must be logged, mask or drop sensitive fields with a small DataWeave expression first; avoid full payload/header logging and exception details that could expose secrets or private data. Mule takes the correlation ID from the source when one is supplied (for example an HTTP `X-Correlation-ID` header); keep it rather than generating a new one. See [correlation ID](https://docs.mulesoft.com/mule-runtime/4.9/correlation-id).
- `log4j2.xml`: keep external appender endpoints and tokens in properties, not literals. On CloudHub 1.0 use only asynchronous appenders, and when logs are forwarded elsewhere keep the `Log4J2CloudhubLogAppender` so logs still reach CloudHub. JSON Logger is a community connector that MuleSoft does not support; use it only if the project already does. See [custom log appenders on CloudHub](https://docs.mulesoft.com/cloudhub-1/custom-log-appender).
- Embedded DataWeave follows [the DataWeave guidance](dataweave.instructions.md). Every changed business/error path needs a meaningful test or an explicit explanation of why it cannot yet be exercised.

## Error handling

- Choose `on-error-propagate` versus `on-error-continue` deliberately at the owning flow or scope. Continue completes its owner successfully; it does not resume at the failed processor. Propagate fails its owner and passes the error outward. Match specific handlers before broad catch-alls. Test the externally observable status/payload and transaction implications. See [error handling](https://docs.mulesoft.com/mule-runtime/4.9/on-error-scope-concept).
- Subflows have no error handler of their own; errors go to the calling flow's handler. To handle an error inside a subflow, wrap the processors in a Try scope.
- Only messaging errors (raised while processing a Mule event) reach `on-error-*` handlers. System errors, such as startup or connection failures with no event, go to a system handler that cannot be configured; address them with reconnection strategies and configuration, not flow handlers. See [system and messaging errors](https://docs.mulesoft.com/mule-runtime/4.9/error-handling).
- Shared handling lives in a named global `<error-handler>`, set as the application default with `<configuration defaultErrorHandler-ref="…"/>` (used by flows that define no handler) or referenced from a flow. Check for both before changing flow-level handlers.
- Raise deliberate failures with `raise-error` using a core type or the project's custom namespace (for example `APP:INVALID_INPUT`); a connector's namespace cannot be used. Processor-level `error-mapping` changes the type handlers see; trace the mapped type before editing a handler. Map APIkit validation errors (`APIKIT:BAD_REQUEST`, `NOT_FOUND`, `METHOD_NOT_ALLOWED`, `NOT_ACCEPTABLE`, `UNSUPPORTED_MEDIA_TYPE`, `NOT_IMPLEMENTED`) to the API's error contract, confirming the set for the project's APIkit version. See [error types and mappings](https://docs.mulesoft.com/mule-runtime/4.9/mule-error-concept).
- Return errors in the shape the API contract defines, with stable error codes callers can branch on; do not invent codes or leak exception text. Without an explicit error response, the HTTP Listener answers 500 with the error description as the body, so set the status and body deliberately (for example through the `httpStatus` variable where the project's APIkit flows use it). See [HTTP Listener](https://docs.mulesoft.com/http-connector/latest/http-listener-ref).

## Architecture and reliability

- If the profile records API-led layers, keep each change inside its layer's role: system APIs expose one system of record, process APIs orchestrate and apply business rules, experience APIs shape data for a consumer. Do not add cross-system orchestration to a system API or direct backend calls to an experience API without an explicit decision.
- Put new shared configuration (connector configs, error handlers, properties) where the project already keeps it, for example a global configuration file, and keep environment-specific values in the project's per-environment property files.
- Scheduler: it uses the host time zone, but UTC on CloudHub unless `timeZone` is set; it runs only on the primary node in a cluster or multi-worker CloudHub deployment; without `disallowConcurrentExecution` a slow run can overlap the next. See [Scheduler](https://docs.mulesoft.com/mule-runtime/4.9/scheduler-concept).
- Polling and redelivery can deliver the same item again: define idempotent handling and check the watermark, unique-ID or post-processing (move/delete) strategy, or use the Idempotent Message Validator with the project's object store. The validator's `idExpression` defaults to `#[correlationId]`; set it to a business key, or a resent message with a new correlation ID will pass. See [Idempotent Message Validator](https://docs.mulesoft.com/mule-runtime/4.9/idempotent-message-validator). With a timestamp watermark, decide how records equal to the watermark are handled (`>` can miss records written in the same instant; `>=` reprocesses them, so processing must be idempotent), and store and compare it at the source column's full precision.
- Streams: repeatable streams are the default. Use `non-repeatable-stream` only when the payload is read exactly once; Cache, Transform, For Each over a JSON array and expressions can all read it. Read or transform a connector's stream promptly: one stored in a variable but never read keeps its connection or file handle until the event ends. A `targetValue` expression must fully consume the stream to release resources at store time; `#[payload]` alone does not. See [streaming](https://docs.mulesoft.com/mule-runtime/4.9/streaming-about).
- Anypoint MQ subscribers: keep acknowledgement tied to successful processing. `AUTO` acknowledges when the flow completes successfully; an error handled with `on-error-continue` can therefore acknowledge failed business work. Work handed to Async is not complete merely because the subscriber flow succeeded. `MANUAL` lets the flow decide; `IMMEDIATE` acknowledges on receipt, so a later failure loses the message. Allow enough acknowledgement time for processing and delays (two minutes when unset), and tolerate redelivery if it expires. Use separate queues per environment and developer. See [Anypoint MQ acknowledgement](https://docs.mulesoft.com/anypoint-mq-connector/4.x/anypoint-mq-ack), [error ownership](https://docs.mulesoft.com/mule-runtime/4.9/on-error-scope-concept) and [Async](https://docs.mulesoft.com/mule-runtime/4.9/async-scope-reference).
- For Each leaves the payload unchanged; Parallel For Each replaces it (or its target) with the collected results of every route and holds them in memory. By default it runs every route at once with no timeout; choose `maxConcurrency` and `timeout` for the contract and downstream capacity. For large volumes, consider Batch only when asynchronous processing and its different result/error contract fit: it does not return processed records to the next processor. Choose by the payload contract and data size, not speed alone. See [Parallel For Each](https://docs.mulesoft.com/mule-runtime/4.9/parallel-foreach-scope) and [Batch processing](https://docs.mulesoft.com/mule-runtime/4.9/batch-processing-concept).
- Design for testing: keep flows and subflows small, with one responsibility each, so each can be tested through its inputs and outputs. Produce `now()`, UUIDs and random values in their own Set Variable rather than inside a Transform, which MUnit cannot mock, so tests can fix them. When a computed request value (query parameter, header or body field) must be checked, compute it into a variable that the connector references, so a test can assert it before the call.
- Consider transforming a collection before For Each only when the post-loop payload, iteration-variable dependencies, error timing and side effects remain equivalent. Combine consecutive Set Variable and Set Payload steps into one Transform only when its outputs are independent; preserve mockable time, UUID and random-value boundaries. Do not log complex DataWeave expressions on every request. See [app design for performance](https://docs.mulesoft.com/mule-runtime/4.9/tuning-app-design) and [independent Transform outputs](https://docs.mulesoft.com/studio/add-another-output-transform-studio-task).
- Async runs its processors on a copy of the event, but the payload objects themselves are shared, so do not mutate them. It returns neither results nor errors to the caller and does not inherit the flow's error handler; put a Try scope inside. See [Async](https://docs.mulesoft.com/mule-runtime/4.9/async-scope-reference).
- Batch jobs: records are processed in blocks (`blockSize` default 100, `maxConcurrency` default twice the cores); use a Batch Aggregator for bulk writes, and consider For Each for small record sets. Record failures are governed by `maxFailedRecords` (default 0 stops the job instance at the first failed record) and each step's `acceptPolicy`/`acceptExpression`, not by the surrounding flow's `on-error-*` handlers. See [batch reference](https://docs.mulesoft.com/mule-runtime/4.9/batch-reference).
- VM queues connect flows within an application and, through shared configuration, separate applications in the same Mule domain. They do not connect separately deployed CloudHub applications. On standalone runtimes the queue type defaults to `TRANSIENT`; `PERSISTENT` serializes messages to disk (or to the memory grid in a cluster). See [VM connector](https://docs.mulesoft.com/vm-connector/latest/). On CloudHub 1.0, messages survive a restart only if Persistent Queues is enabled for the application; it adds tens of milliseconds per message and does not guarantee one-time delivery, so consumers must tolerate duplicates. See [persistent queues](https://docs.mulesoft.com/cloudhub-1/managing-queues).
- Cache scope: by default the cache key is a SHA-256 hash of the payload, so when the result depends on attributes, variables or the caller's identity, define the key in a caching strategy. Only repeatable streams are cached. Cache only data that changes rarely, use a configured object store with an expiry, invalidate entries when the source changes, and never let one caller's data be served to another. See [Cache scope](https://docs.mulesoft.com/mule-runtime/4.9/cache-scope).

## Deployment target specifics

Apply the rules for the target recorded in the profile.

- CloudHub 1.0: HTTP listeners use host `0.0.0.0` and the reserved `${http.port}` (8081) or `${https.port}` (8082) properties for shared-load-balancer traffic. Private services use `${http.private.port}`/`${https.private.port}` (8091/8092), reachable directly within the application's Anypoint VPC or through a configured dedicated load balancer. A private port alone does not establish the intended exposure: check VPC firewall rules and any dedicated-load-balancer allowlist. Never hard-code these ports. See [CloudHub networking](https://docs.mulesoft.com/cloudhub-1/cloudhub-networking-guide).
- Multi-worker CloudHub and clusters: keep no state in memory or local files between requests. CloudHub worker disk is ephemeral and cleared on restart, including files written by the File connector. Use the project's object store. Object Store v2 stays in the region where the app was first deployed, limits values to 10 MB and keys to 1,024 bytes, and rate-limits each app. Check the configured TTL: static TTL is capped at 30 days, while rolling TTL can retain entries beyond 30 days. Object Store v2 provides no distributed locking across CloudHub workers; concurrent shared-key updates need an explicit synchronization design. See the [Object Store v2 overview](https://docs.mulesoft.com/object-store/) and [FAQ](https://docs.mulesoft.com/object-store/osv2-faq).
- Clustered sources: JMS topic listeners receive only on the primary node by default and queue listeners on all nodes; setting `primaryNodeOnly="false"` on a topic without shared subscriptions processes each message once per node. In Mule 4 clusters, File, FTP and SFTP use distributed polling by default. See [JMS in clusters](https://docs.mulesoft.com/jms-connector/latest/jms-performance) and [distributed file polling](https://docs.mulesoft.com/mule-runtime/4.9/distributed-file-polling).
- API Manager: keep any `api-gateway:autodiscovery` element. Its `apiId` comes from a per-environment property, and its `flowRef` must name the flow with the HTTP Listener. Organization credentials are configured on the runtime or deployment, never in the repository. See [API Autodiscovery](https://docs.mulesoft.com/api-manager/latest/configure-autodiscovery-4-task).
- Standalone runtimes: a Mule domain project can share connector configurations (for example one HTTP listener port), properties and scheduler pools across applications on the same runtime, but not flows, subflows or message processors. Domains cannot be installed through Runtime Manager, so they do not apply to CloudHub. See [shared resources](https://docs.mulesoft.com/mule-runtime/4.9/shared-resources).
